clips.title: Welcome — what MEL really means
clips.speaker: Varna
clips.transcript: Hi folks, my name is Varna and a very warm welcome to all of you. Super happy to see you all here at ImpactMojo. Every year, organizations across South Asia spend crores collecting data on the programs they run: attendance sheets, beneficiary accounts, workshop photos. Most of it goes into a report, gets sent to a funder and sits there unread by December. That kind of data collection serves compliance. It really really serves decisions. MEL, as we all know, stands for monitoring, evaluation, and learning. Monitoring tracks whether a program is running as planned, are the supplements arriving, are the sessions happening, do the numbers match the work plan. Evaluation asks whether the program is achieving what it set out to achieve and for whom. Learning is what an organization does with those answers, feeding evaluation findings back into how the next field. ways gets designed. So the first takeaway, MEL exists to improve decisions. Take a nutrition program distributing supplements to children under 5. Monitoring tells you how many children received supplements this month, which matters to whoever manages the supply chain. What it doesn't do is it says nothing about whether nutritional status improved. Evaluation asks that question directly and it asks a harder one alongside it. Did nutritional status improve more for the children in this program than for children who were never reached by it at all. A program officer deciding whether to expand into three more blocks needs that second answer. The monitoring number on its own will not tell her whether expansion is worth the money. Second takeaway, MEL is not reporting, though the two get confused constantly. Reporting is retrospective. It documents what already happened, usually in a format under a specified condition and a specified way. Usually months after the events it describes. A mail system built properly runs alongside the program rather than actually trailing behind it. It gets designed from month 1, not assembled in month 11, because the annual report deadline is approaching. A program that waits until month 11 to build its mail system has already lost the chance to catch a failing activity back in month 3 while there was still time to fix it. By month Month 11, the year is spent and a report can only record what already went wrong. Third takeaway, good mail treats causality as a question to answer, not an assumption to make. Take literacy scores that rise in a district the same year an NGO runs a reading program there. Crediting the program is tempting, but scores could rise because the state issued new textbooks that year, because a good monsoon kept attendance steady through the term. or because of several other things moving in that district at the same time. So causal thinking asks what would have happened in the program's absence. Real comparison, a control group, a match district, a credible baseline measured before the program started. A rise in scores that happens near a program's timeline with no comparison behind it tells you very, very little. The same rise measured against a real counterfactual tells you what the program actually did. Mail exists to improve decisions. It is not the same activity as reporting and it treats causality as something to establish, not something to assume. We have a full course on this at impactmojo.in. Vandana should be able to share the link with you. It goes further into monitoring system design, evaluation methods and how to build learning loops that teams actually use rather than the ones that only get open during a donor review. I hope this video on what MEL is and why it matters, um, you know, serves as a useful, let's say 3-minute introduction and I look forward to a lot of our conversations going forward here. Thank you so much for joining.

clips.title: When your Theory of Change is just paperwork
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript:
Yes, this is one of the most common gaps in the sector and I have actually fixed it in practice. For example, I worked with a livelihood organization in Bihar whose TOC existed on paper but got treated as a funding document. So nobody consulted it between proposal cycles. The fix was actually not to rewrite the TOC, it was to tie each assumption in it to something the team already actually collected in their own MIS. So the the assumption that training, for example, leads to income improvement stopped sitting on a page unquestioned and became a line that the team checked against their own data every quarter.
So here's what changed on the ground, right?
Staff started naming out loud when the logic broke between an activity and its assumed outcome.
That is the actual test of whether a TOC functions as a learning tool rather than paperwork.
So if a field worker can point going to the exact step where an assumption failed last quarter.
The document is alive in that sense.
If it only gets opened for a donor visit, it's dead weight with a nice diagram.
So for small NGOs, the constraint is bandwidth, strong willingness.
Two things that actually head up in my memory in that project.
First, put the TOC review inside a meeting that already exists, like a monthly review or a quarterly board update, rather rather than inventing some kind of new ritual that nobody has the time for. And second, bring field staff into the room when the TOC gets revised, not only whoever wrote the original proposal or management. Field staff actually see where the logic fails in practice because they are the ones standing in the gap between the activity and the outcome every day. So if anyone on this AMA wants a structured way to work through this, ImpactMojo's flagship course which is free, the evidence question, monitoring evaluation. and learning for practice, covers TOC design and assumption mapping directly, and the TOC workbench lab gives you the opportunity and the place to build one out rather than just read about it.

clips.title: When five trackers won't add up
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript: Hi, this is a stage most MEL systems hit somewhere between 15 and 50 field staff. So this is a familiar bottleneck. It's not a beginner mistake. The core issue is the absence of one participant list that every program tracker refers back to. So if each of your five interventions keeps its own separate name list, you will end up with several different spellings of the same child across several. sheets. There is no way to check afterward whether your reported numbers count one child five times or five children once. Fix this before touching any dashboard. Build a master roster, I'd say with a unique ID assigned to each participant at enrollment and have every program sheet carry that ID as a column. Nothing else as identifier. That single ID is what eventually lets five separate trackers sit under one dashboard instead of existing as five unrelated files. Once the ID system exists, move data entry of shared Excel and onto a form tools such as KoBo Toolbox or Google Forms, all of which are free, feeding into sheets. Shared Excel with 40 people editing simultaneously fails in specific predictive ways. Someone overwrites a formula, someone enters a date as text instead of a date field, someone inserts a column and every downstream reference shifts one by one and nobody Nobody notices until the totals stop adding up. A form locks the structure, so a team member assigned to one program cannot enter data into another program's field by mistake. So there are programs like KoBo Toolbox for example that also supports skip logic. So each program's form only shows its questions to whoever is filling it in that day. Um, for the dashboard layer, I'd say Power BI connected live to your sheets works well at scale. There is budget for the license and the learning curve. ImpactMojo runs a course called Power BI for practitioners covering star schema design, Power Query cleaning steps and visualization using real survey data built for people without a data background. If cost is tight, a well-built pivot table structure in one master sheet pulling from the 5 program sheets by participant ID gets you most of the same value for close to no cost. Structure the dashboard, I'd say, in three layers: total reach across all five interventions at the top, program level numbers below that, indicator level only on click through. One step before building any of this is sit with each of your five program leads and get them to name the two or three indicators per intervention that would actually change a decision if the number moved. Systems built around what is easy to collect rather than what is needed to decide something terrifying. tend to collapse within a couple of quarters because nobody has the time to review 40 indicators a month. And the ones nobody reviews are the ones that stop being entered accurately. So if you want a structured way to design the indicator side, ImpactMojos MEL framework workbench lab is actually built for that step.

clips.title: What makes a good indicator?
clips.speaker: ImpactMojo
clips.transcript: Indicators, what makes a good one. An implementing partner reports that it distributed 40000 textbooks this year. The number is real, it is measurable and it goes straight into the quarterly report. What it does not tell you is whether a single child read a page further because of it. The gap between what gets counted and what actually matters is where most indicator design goes wrong. First takeaway, a good indicator measures what actually matters for the decision at hand, not what happens to be easy to count. Textbooks distributed is easy. Someone can count boxes at a warehouse. Reading comprehension improved is hard. It needs a test, administered consistently to a sample of children, compared against some kind of baseline. Programs gravitate towards the easy number because it is cheap and because it always moves in a reassuring direction. correction. Distribution figures only go up. The harder number is the one a decision maker actually needs before deciding whether to fund a second print run or redesign the whole approach. Second takeaway. Smart is necessary, but it's not sufficient. Every med training covers the smart criteria that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time bound. We all know this, right? They are worth knowing. going and an indicator that fails them is broken from the start. But smart only checks the shape of an indicator. It says nothing about whether the indicator is actually tracking the thing you care about. Number of training sessions held is specific. It's measurable, it's achievable, it's relevant to a training program and it's time bound to the reporting period. It is also almost useless for telling you whether the training changed anyone's behavior. Smart gets your well-formed indicator. It does not Get you a meaningful one. Third takeaway. Once an indicator becomes a target, people start optimizing for the indicator rather than the outcome it was meant to represent or what it was intended to achieve. This is sometimes called good hearts law after the economist who first stated it in the context of monetary policy. But the pattern shows up constantly in development work. Tell field staff that their performance is judged on the number of households in the country. visited and the household visits will rise. Sometimes by recording visits that lasted 90 seconds and covered well almost nothing. Tell teachers that attendance figures matter for a school's ranking and attendance registers can start looking really good, better than the classroom does. None of this requires bad faith. What happens is that when a proxy actually replaces the goal quietly and nobody actually notices the substitution because the number goes on the dashboard, they keep improving. But the three together and the practical test for any indicator is this. Does it track something a decision actually depends on? Does it hold up as a well-formed measure and can it survive becoming a target without collapsing into something that people can quietly gain. An indicator that passes the first two tests and fails the third will still mislead you just a little more slowly. The full The full course should be in a link that Vandana can share below. It covers an indicator design in more depth along with the sampling and baseline decisions that determine whether an indicator can even be interpreted once the data comes in or perhaps at a different time point. Happy reading. Please stay with us at Impact Motor.

clips.title: Baseline design — the decisions that matter
clips.speaker: ImpactMojo
clips.transcript: Hello, today we're talking about baseline design and the decisions that matter. A baseline is often treated as a formality to go out before the program starts, collect some numbers, file them away, move on to implementation. Done that way, unfortunately, a baseline is close to worthless. The decisions made at baseline stage determine whether anything collected afterward can actually be interpreted, and most of those decisions get made in the first two weeks of a project under time pressure by whoever happens to be available. at that particular point in time. So the first takeaway, a baseline without a counterfactual is just a photograph or at least close enough. A photograph tells you what conditions look like at one point in time. It does not tell you what would have happened without the program. If literacy rates in a district were 40% before an intervention and 50% two years later, that 10 point rise means very little on its own. Rates could have risen anyway from a new textbook policy from a good run of school attendance, you know, from a state government scheme, maybe a growth effect of the child itself running in parallel. A baseline earns the name only when it is paired with a comparison group, a control, a math set of villages or schools that did not receive the program, so that the 10 point rise can be checked against what happened in places the program never touched or where it never happened at all. Without that comparison, a baseline records a starting point and enough nothing more. Kind of like knowing where a day starts but not much else. Second takeaway, sampling choices made at baseline constraint everything downstream and they are close to impossible to fix later. If the baseline sample skews towards villages near a main road for example because they were easier to reach, every end line comparison inherits that skew. If a matched comparison group was selected using criteria that turn out to differ from the treatment group in some Some way that matters no amount of statistical adjustment fully repairs at that end line. Sample size decided at baseline sets the limit on what effect sizes the evaluation will ever be able to detect with any confidence and that limit does not move no matter how good the end line fieldwork is. These are not decisions to delegate to whoever is free at that point in time in that week. They need someone who understands what the evaluation is meant to detect, deciding beforehand. before a single household is visited because a sampling frame that is built on wrong logic cannot be corrected after the fact. It can only be lived with and that pain will never go away. Third takeaway, document your methodology, not your numbers. 2 years after a baseline, someone will ask how the comparison group was selected, what the exact wording of a key question was, whether a particular village was excluded. and why. If the answer lives only in the memory of whoever ran the field work, and that person has since left, moved on, or gone to a different organization, the baseline becomes unusable at exactly the moment it was supposed to be off, which is at the end line when it needs to be compared with something. A spreadsheet of baseline numbers without a methodology note or context attached to a set of figures, nobody can defend under scrutiny. The note should record the sample. sampling frame, the selection criteria for any comparison group, the exact survey instrument used, and any deviations from the original design because there are always some deviations. That documentation is what turns a baseline from a fixed artifact into evidence that can withstand quite a serious question 2 years later. Taking together these three decisions, the counterfactual, the sampling design, and the documentation. are what separate a baseline that supports a real evaluation from one that produces a number that nobody can trust once anyone asks how was it built. We have a course which is again you know on sampling in particular and evaluation design. Vandana should be able to share the link of the series and the rest of the advanced track with you. Stay with ImpactMojo. Happy learning.

If you cannot name one, your system is producing accountability, which I think is a legitimate function, but it's not the same thing as learning. Now the second point, and this is where I think most of us get stuck, right? Learning is not the same as completing an evaluation, checking a box, right? An evaluation is an event. It has a TOR, an inception report, a field phase, a draft, maybe a validation workshop, a final report. Everyone involved is heavily incentivized to kind of finish it, complete it, report it, done. Almost nobody incentivized for what happens after it. The report lands in April, the program design was locked in in the previous November. The next design window, it opens in 18 months from now. So the evaluation can be technically excellent and still arrive at a moment when no decision is open. The finding has actually, how do I say this plainly? It has nowhere to go. So this is Patton's old argument in utilization focused evaluation. And it has been sitting there since 1978 without being taken seriously enough. What Patton asks you is to identify the specific people who will use the findings and the specific decisions they face before you design anything at all. Named people. real decisions with real dates, which brings me to the third point. Learning is a scheduled activity, otherwise it's fiction. So think about how ruthlessly we schedule everything else, right, in our lives. Or even in M&E, baseline in month three, midline in month 18, quarterly reports on the 15th, all of it is in the work plan. And all All of it is costly, all of it with somebody's name on it. Then learning kind of goes or gets into ongoing reflection and no budget line. Put it in the calendar instead, a quarterly session, 90 minutes with two or three people who can actually authorize a change to how the program is being rolled out. Bring three findings, not 30, not 50. For each one, the question on the table is, does this change what we do next quarter? Yes or no? If the answer is no, say so loudly, and you also need to record why. That's a legitimate outcome. We looked and we are staying the course, and here is our reason. This is a learning record. Silence on why a decision took place or didn't is not. One more thing. worth saying because it is uncomfortable. A lot of what gets called learning in our sector is retrospective justification. The program design was set by a donor's theory of change or by what the last grant funded or by what the team already knows how to do. The M&E data arrives afterwards and then it gets read for evidence that the choice was made. actually found, but was it? Everyone recognizes this when it happens elsewhere. And nobody actually recognizes it in their own project or their own program that they're taking ownership for. The defense against it is boring and it's procedural. Write it down before the data comes in. What results would make you kind of change course. Then check whether that result actually arrived, did it actually happen on the ground. This is learning. Everything else, in my view, is reporting.

clips.title: Designing gender-sensitive FGDs and KIIs
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript:
Hi everyone. Welcome to PLC Group. Today, in this microlearning video, we will talk about designing gender-sensitive focus group discussions and key informant interviews. When we say gender-sensitive research, we often think about one thing first: do we include both women and men in our sample? But gender-sensitive qualitative research is much more than that. Because in an FGD or KII, who is in the room, who is asking the question, and how the conversation is structured can all shape the evidence we get. So here are three things to think about when designing gender-sensitive FGDs and KIIs.

Takeaway one: who you include determines what you can learn. Before designing your FGD or KII, don't just ask, "Who is your target population?" Ask, "Whose experience do we need to understand?" For example, if you're studying girls' access to secondary education, talking only to girls may tell you about their experience. But talking separately to girls, boys, parents, teachers and school leaders may reveal something different about gender norms and power relationships shaping those experiences. And importantly, don't assume that women or men are homogeneous groups. Age, caste, class, disability, marital status, geography, sexuality, occupation and other social identities can intersect with gender. So your sampling should reflect the differences that matter for your research question. UN Women specifically emphasises that gender-sensitive data collection needs to reflect the realities of different groups, and that qualitative methods such as KIIs and FGDs can be used to surface these differences.

Takeaway two: who is in the room changes what is said. This is particularly important for FGDs. Imagine asking adolescent girls about mobility restrictions in a group that includes their father, male teachers, or community leaders. Will they speak in exactly the same way? Probably not. Because power relations, social expectation, and concerns about judgment can influence what people are willing to disclose. That is why group composition matters. You may need separate groups based on gender, age, social position and other characteristics, particularly when discussing sensitive issues. And don't forget the facilitator. The gender, age, social position and perceived authority of the interviewer can also influence the interaction. There is research from Bihar, for example, that explored how interviewers' gender affected women's responses to questions about household and maternal health, highlighting that interviewer characteristics can matter in traditional settings. So don't treat the facilitator as invisible. The researcher is part of the research environment.

Takeaway three: how you ask determines what becomes visible. A gender-sensitive interview guide is not simply "What problems do women face?" That question already assumes women have problems and may completely miss the underlying system. Instead, can we ask questions that explore roles, expectations, decision-making and power? For example, instead of "Do women participate in household financial decisions?", let's try "Who usually makes decisions about how household money is spent? Can you give an example of a recent decision?" Then you can probe further and ask: who was consulted? Who had the final say? Would this be different for a man, a woman or a third-gender person in the same situation? These questions move us from individual characteristics to relationships, norms and structure, and that's often where gender becomes visible.

And finally, remember that FGDs and KIIs serve different purposes. FGDs are particularly useful for understanding shared norms, language, expectation, and differences within a group. KIIs can help us understand institutions, systems, decision-making, and the perspective of people with particular knowledge or role. So before your next FGD or KII, pause and ask three questions. Who needs to be in the room? Who might speak differently because of who else is in the room? And what questions will help us uncover gendered roles, norms and power, rather than simply document differences between women, men and third gender? Because gender-sensitive qualitative research isn't just about collecting data from women and men. It is about designing the research so that gendered experiences and power relationships have a chance to become visible. Thank you, and have a great week.

clips.title: What gender-sensitive MEL actually asks
clips.speaker: Vandana
clips.transcript:
Hi everyone, hope you are reading and enjoying and learning from the PLC group. Today let's talk about what gender-sensitive MEL is. When we say gender-sensitive MEL, many of us immediately think we need to disaggregate our data by sex. So we count how many women participated, how many men participated. And yes, that is important. But gender-sensitive MEL goes beyond counting. Because knowing that sixty percent of participants were women doesn't tell us whether women actually had equal access, benefited equally, or experienced the programme in the same way.

Let's take a simple example. Imagine a hundred people attend a skill training programme. Sixty are women. Great. We might say women's participation is strong. But then we ask: did women attend regularly? Did they have time to participate alongside unpaid care and household responsibilities? Did they have access to transport or digital devices? After training, were they able to use those skills? And if they earned an income, did they have control over that income? Now we are asking gender-sensitive MEL questions.

Gender-sensitive MEL recognises that gender is not just a category in our data. Gender shapes people's roles, access to resources, decision-making, time, mobility and power. So instead of asking only how many men or women participated, we also ask: did women and men experience the programme differently? If so, why? And did the programme change anything about these differences?

This also changes what we measure. For example, instead of only measuring how many women received financial support, we might also ask how many women have independent access to and control over that support. Instead of just counting women in a community meeting, we ask: were women able to speak? Were their views included in the decisions? So we move from measuring participation to understanding access, benefit, voice, control and power.

And finally, gender-sensitive MEL is not just about collecting better data. It is about using what we learn to adapt our programmes. If we find that women are dropping out because sessions clash with their care responsibilities, what do we change? If women participate but don't control the benefits, what do we need to redesign? That's when MEL becomes a tool for gender equality, not just for reporting.

So here's a key takeaway. Sex-disaggregated data tells us who participated. Gender-sensitive MEL asks how gender shaped their experiences, outcomes and power, and what we need to do differently because of what we find. And here, when we say gender, we mean men, women and other third-gender categories. For this week's PLC discussion, I would welcome all of us to take one indicator from your own programme and ask: what am I missing if I only disaggregate this data by gender? Thank you, and have a great weekend.
